paragraphs.text: People who owe a daily tax to their rulers, if the debt has gone unpaid for several days, settle all the separate arrears at once in a single sum as soon as they come into some money. I will do the same with your reverence. I owe you frequent letters, since for Christians a promise is a debt. Through no wish of my own I have fallen behind with them, and I now want to make up for it by stretching this letter to such a length that, if it were divided into letters of the usual size, it would count as many. But so that a long letter does not become idle chatter, I think it best to use this written voice to imitate our conversations face to face. You surely remember that our talks with each other always began from the study of virtue and training in godliness. You would always

listen closely and raise objections to what was said, accepting nothing without examining it, while I, being the elder, would resolve whatever questions came up as the argument went on. If it were possible to do the same now, so that your wisdom supplied the starting point for the discussion, that would be far better. We would both gain twice over: from seeing each other, which for me is the sweetest thing in life, and from having my aged lyre stirred into sound by your understanding, as if by a plectrum. But since the necessities of life keep us apart in body, though we are joined in soul, I will have to take on your part as well, wherever some objection to the argument might come up as it proceeds. It would be good to set before this letter some subject that profits the soul, and then to give the discussion over to it.

Let us then examine, as if it were a set problem, the question: What does the Christian profess? Perhaps an inquiry into this will not be without profit. For if we discover exactly what this name signifies, we will gain great help toward a life of virtue, striving through an exalted way of life truly to be what we are called. If someone wanted to be called a physician, an orator or a geometer, he would not want his lack of training to expose the title as false when, put to the test, he turned out not to be what he was called. Whoever wants to be called any of these things in truth will confirm the title by actually practicing the art, so that the name is not shown to be a false one. In the same way, if we examine and find the true aim of the Christian profession, we would not choose to be anything other than what the name professes on our behalf. Otherwise the story about the ape that circulates among the pagans might fit us too.

They say that a showman in the city of Alexandria trained an ape, by some kind of nimbleness, to strike dancing poses. He put a dancer's mask on it and clothes suited to the art, set a chorus around it, and won great fame with the ape as it twisted itself to the rhythm of the music and in everything it did and seemed to be concealed its own nature. While the theater was spellbound by the novelty of the spectacle, a wit who was present showed those gaping at it, by way of a joke, that the ape was an ape. As everyone was shouting and applauding the ape's turns while it moved in time with the song and the music, they say he threw onto the stage the kind of sweets that tempt the greed of such animals. The ape did not hesitate for a moment: as soon as it saw the almonds scattered in front of the chorus, it forgot the stage, the

applause and its fine costume, ran over to them and gathered up what it found in its paws. And so that the mask would not get in the way of its mouth, it hastily pulled it off, tearing apart the cleverly made face with its claws. At once, instead of praise and admiration, it moved the spectators to laughter, as it showed itself ugly and ridiculous among the shreds of the mask. That cleverly made disguise was not enough to make the ape pass for a man, once its nature was exposed by its greed for the sweets. In the same way, those who have not truly shaped their very nature by faith will easily be exposed by the devil's temptations as something other than what they profess to be. For instead of a fig or an almond or the like, vainglory and ambition, love of gain and love of pleasure, and everything else of the kind that the devil's evil market sets out like sweets before greedy people, easily expose those apish souls who play at Christianity by putting on an imitation. In the moment of passion they destroy their mask of self-control, or meekness, or some other virtue. So we must understand what Christianity professes. Then perhaps we may become what the name means, so that we are not shown before him who sees what is hidden to be something other than we appear, shaped only by a bare confession and the outward show of a name.

First, then, let us consider what Christianity means from the name itself. Wiser men may well find some greater and loftier meaning, in keeping with the sublimity of the name. But what we are able to grasp about this name is this. The name Christ, if translated into a clearer and more familiar word, means king, since holy Scripture, by a usage of its own, indicates royal dignity by this term. But since, as Scripture says, the Divine is ineffable and incomprehensible, beyond every concept that could grasp it, the prophets and apostles, who were inspired by the Holy Spirit, have of necessity led us by the hand toward an understanding of the incorruptible nature with many names and concepts, one directing us to one concept worthy of God, another to another. Thus authority over all things is indicated by the name of kingship, while freedom from and the absence of all passion and all evil is named by the names of the virtues, each understood and spoken of in its highest sense. So the same one is righteousness and wisdom and power and truth, goodness and life and salvation and incorruption, unchangeable and unalterable; and every

lofty concept signified by such names, Christ both is and is called. If, then, every lofty concept is understood as comprised in the name of Christ (for the others are contained in the loftiest of the meanings, so that each of them is seen within the idea of kingship), perhaps we may arrive by logical sequence at an understanding of what Christianity means. For if we who are joined to him through faith in him are named together with the highest of the names that interpret the incorruptible nature, it follows necessarily that we should also share by consequence in the names of all the concepts contemplated in that incorruptible nature together with this name. As we have received the name Christian by sharing in Christ, so it is fitting that we should consequently draw along with it a share in all the lofty names. When someone pulls the end link of a chain, he draws along with that one link all the links attached to it. In the same way, since the other names that interpret that ineffable and manifold blessedness are attached to the name of Christ, whoever grasps the one must necessarily draw the rest along with it. So if anyone takes on the name of Christ but does not show in his life all that is contemplated together with this name, he belies the name. To follow the example we put forward, he puts on the ape a lifeless mask fashioned in human likeness. For Christ cannot fail to be righteousness and purity and truth and estrangement from all evil; nor can anyone be a Christian (that is, a true Christian) without showing in himself a share in those names as well. If one were to set out the meaning of Christianity in a definition, then, we will say this: Christianity is the imitation of the divine nature.

Let no one attack this definition as extravagant and as overstepping the lowliness of our nature, for the definition has not gone beyond our nature. If anyone considers the original state of man, he will find from the teachings of Scripture that the definition has not exceeded the limits of our nature. For the first creation of man was in imitation of God's likeness (so Moses taught in his philosophy about man, when he says, "God made man; in the image of God he made him"), and what Christianity promises is that man will be restored to his ancient happy state.
If man was originally the likeness of God, perhaps we have not missed the mark in our definition when we declared Christianity to be the imitation of the divine nature. The promise of the name, then,

is this great. It is time to consider whether it is without danger for one who puts the name forward not to live accordingly. What we are looking for may become clear from an example. Suppose someone professes the art of painting, and the ruler orders him to depict the king's likeness for those who live far away. If he scrawls some hideous and misshapen figure on the panel and calls this ugly form the king's portrait, would the sovereign not rightly be indignant that his original beauty is insulted by that bad painting among those who do not know him? For whatever form is shown in the image, the original form must also be thought to be like it. So if the definition says that Christianity is the imitation of God, anyone who has not yet received the teaching of the mystery will suppose that our God is just like the life he sees in us, which is believed to be lived in imitation of God. If he sees examples of every good, he will believe that the God we worship is good. But if someone is passionate and bestial, shaped in his character now into one animal's form and now into another's (for one can plainly see beasts taking shape in the perversions of our nature), and then such a person calls himself a Christian, when it is evident to all that the promise of the name professes the imitation of God, he will by his own life make the God we believe in an object of blame among unbelievers. That is why Scripture pronounces a rather fearful threat against such people, saying: "Woe to those through whom my name is blasphemed among the nations." And I think the Lord is leading us chiefly to this meaning when he says to those able to hear it: "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." For in calling the true Father the Father of those who have believed, he wants those born through him to resemble the perfection of good things seen in him.

You will say to me, then: "How can human lowliness reach out toward the blessedness seen in God, when the very command plainly shows the thing to be impossible? How could the earthly become like the one in heaven, when the very difference in nature shows that such imitation is out of reach? It is just as impossible for a man of earth to be made like the heavenly God as it is for one's figure to be made equal to the vastness of heaven and the beauties in it." But the answer to this is clear. The Gospel does not command that human nature be compared with the divine nature, but that we imitate its good activities in our life as far as possible. What, then, are the activities of ours that resemble the activities of God? To be estranged from all evil as far as possible, keeping ourselves pure of its defilements in deed, word and thought. This is truly the imitation of the divine perfection, the perfection of the heavenly God.

For I do not think that when the Gospel commands us to be made perfect after the pattern of the heavenly Father it means the element of heaven, as though it were a separate dwelling of God. The Divine is present in all things equally and pervades the whole of creation alike, and nothing could remain in existence if it were separated from him who is. The divine nature touches each existing thing in equal measure, enclosing all things within itself by its all-embracing power. The Prophet teaches this too, saying in effect: "Whether I am in heaven, whether I go beneath the earth, whether I stretch the thinking of my soul to the very limits of what exists, I see all things [held?] in your right hand." The actual wording runs like this: "If I go up into heaven, you are there; if I go down into Hades, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest reaches of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me." From this, then, we can learn that the heavenly dwelling has not been set apart for God as his special abode. But it is known that the realm above is pure of evil (holy Scripture indicates this to us in many places through riddles), while in this more material life the deeds of evil are carried out, since the inventor of evil, the serpent, crawls and creeps about earthly life. As the word says of him in a riddle, he goes on his breast and belly and eats earth continually. This explains to us both the manner of his movement and the kind of food he eats: it is this earthly, low-lying life that receives upon itself the creeping of manifold evil and becomes food for the beast that creeps over it. So he who commands us to imitate the heavenly Father commands us to be pure of earthly passions. Departure from these is accomplished not by moving from place to place but by choice alone. If, then, estrangement from evil is naturally achieved by the impulse of the mind alone, the word of the Gospel lays on us nothing laborious. No toil is attached to the impulse of the mind; we can be wherever we wish through our thoughts without any trouble. So it is easy for anyone who wishes to have the heavenly way of life even on earth, as the Gospel teaches, by setting his mind on heavenly things and laying up the wealth of virtue in the treasuries there. "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth," it says, "but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal." By this he shows that no power destructive of blessedness has a place in the life above. For he who, to ruin our life here, works his manifold evil against human life in many ways

either breeds in our thoughts like a moth, making useless whatever part he grows in; or by his corroding and consuming power, unless he is quickly shaken off that part, creeps on to what lies next to it, and as he moves leaves the mark of decay on whatever he approaches; or, if what is within is secure, he lays his plots through outward circumstances. Either he breaks through the wall into the treasury of the heart by means of pleasure, or by some other passion he empties the vessel of the soul of virtue, stealing away our reason through anger or grief or some other such passion. Since the Lord says that in the treasuries above there is neither moth nor rust, nor the evil of the thief, which teaches the things we have just considered, we must move our trading there. There whatever has been stored up not only remains forever safe and undiminished, but also, like seeds, yields an increase many times over. For the return must surely be magnified according to the nature of the one who receives the deposit. Just as we act according to our own nature, offering poor gifts because that is what we are, so it is fitting that he who is rich in everything should repay those who have given to him first with the things that are his by nature. So let no one lose heart, as he contributes what he can to the divine treasuries, thinking that he will receive back only as much as he gave. Let him wait instead, according to the promise of the one who said that he will exchange great things for small, giving heavenly things for earthly and eternal things for short-lived ones. These things are such by nature that they cannot be grasped by thought or put into words. Of them the divinely inspired Scripture teaches: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him."

This, my honored friend, is what I have sent you, not only to make up for the letters I failed to write but also as payment in advance for the shortfalls to come. May you fare in the Lord as you wish. And may your wish always be what is pleasing to God and dear to us.
